summary: A modular monolith build: React SPA on the frontend, Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on AWS ECS on Fargate. About $1,945-7,310 a month. With 8 engineer(s), one deployable with strict internal module boundaries is the fastest and cheapest to run; modules can be extracted into services later.

frontend.choice: React SPA (Vite) + Native iOS + Android (Swift / Kotlin) for the Android/iOS app
frontend.justification: React SPA (Vite) is the frontend for a Fintech / payments / ledger project with about 60,000 daily users (~833 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 8 in 16 weeks. Search visibility is marked not needed (behind login), so rendering in the browser is acceptable, and it scores 5.0/5 for rich, app-like interaction. Angular is within 0.8 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied), so either is defensible (see the runner-up note). You also target iOS/Android. Native iOS + Android (Swift / Kotlin) scored best among mobile toolkits with the same weights and backend.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.8 points higher; either is defensible. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), development speed (4.0 vs 3.0); Angular is stronger on structure for large teams (5.0 vs 2.0), team skill match (4.0 vs 3.5).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.2 points. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files.
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)

tradeoffs: Client-side rendering hurts SEO and first paint on slow phones
Routing, data fetching and state are your own architecture decisions

backend.justification: Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot serves the API at about 833 requests/s at peak (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)) for a team of 8. It runs as a long-running Java/Kotlin service, so background jobs, WebSockets and database connection pools live in one deployable process. It leads the runner-up, Go (net/http, chi or Gin), by 3.0 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.0 points. Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on team skill match (5.0 vs 3.5), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0); Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 4.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.5 points. Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (5.0 vs 1.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on low ops burden (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (4.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 7.1 points. Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on team skill match (5.0 vs 1.5), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 3.0), low ops burden (4.0 vs 3.0); Python + Django takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Python or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn.

database.choice: PostgreSQL: Amazon RDS / Aurora PostgreSQL (+ RDS Proxy for serverless)
database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 500 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. You need strong consistency, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. Its share of the estimated bill is $800-$1,600 a month, against a total budget of $6,000 a month. MySQL is within 0.1 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied), so either is defensible (see the runner-up note).

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.1 points lower; either is defensible. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 6.8 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on data-model fit (5.0 vs 2.0), consistency fit (5.0 vs 3.5); MongoDB is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Only 2/5 fit for your primary 'relational' data.
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data; In-memory store: ~500 GB within 12 months cannot sensibly live in RAM as the system of record (use it as a cache)
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data

tradeoffs: Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless
Nobody on the team listed PostgreSQL or a closely related skill; plan 2-4 weeks to learn it.

hosting.choice: AWS ECS on Fargate, region ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
hosting.justification: AWS ECS on Fargate hosts the stack for users in India at a 99.95% availability target. It runs the Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot API as long-running processes, sized for ~833 requests/s at peak. For PCI DSS it is a validated service provider, so card-handling infrastructure can sit on it. Its share of the estimated bill is $800-$4,000 a month, against a total budget of $6,000 a month. It leads the runner-up, AWS Lambda + API Gateway, by 2.9 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.9 points. AWS ECS on Fargate is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), portability (low lock-in) (3.0 vs 2.0); AWS Lambda + API Gateway is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0).
Ruled out for your answers: Not on AWS, the cloud you require.

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path.

supporting.choice: Amazon S3 (a separate bucket for uploaded files, served through the same CloudFront as the static frontend)
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database.

supporting.choice: CDN in front of the object storage, with image resizing at the edge
supporting.justification: Serve uploads from the CDN, not the app server; resize images on the fly instead of storing every size.

supporting.choice: MSG91 or Twilio Verify, with DLT-registered SMS templates
supporting.justification: One-time codes need an SMS gateway with rate limits against SMS-pumping fraud; Indian operators deliver only DLT-registered templates.

supporting.choice: Razorpay / Cashfree (India) or Stripe with hosted checkout (card tokens)
supporting.justification: Card data never touches your servers, which keeps your PCI-DSS audit scope to the smallest self-assessment form (SAQ A).

React SPA is built to static files (HTML, JavaScript, CSS): a bucket behind the cloud's CDN serves them from the edge, so the Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot instances on AWS ECS on Fargate only answer API calls, and a frontend release is an upload plus a cache invalidation.

supporting.choice: Amazon Cognito in the Mumbai region
supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO.

supporting.choice: Firebase Cloud Messaging (+ APNs) or Expo Notifications
supporting.justification: Standard channel for mobile engagement on Android and iOS.

supporting.choice: Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint for your own model (Amazon Bedrock for a hosted one)
supporting.justification: Serve the model from its own endpoint, versioned and monitored apart from the web tier; a small scoring model runs on CPU.
Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target.

supporting.choice: Encrypted storage (KMS), audit logging, least-privilege IAM, WAF
supporting.justification: PCI-DSS requires access controls, audit trails and encryption.

assumptions: Planning estimate from published price bands at your scale tier, with the usage terms listed per line; excludes salaries, third-party SaaS (auth, email, payments fees) and egress spikes.
Scale tier: Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)
Budget check: $6,000/month stated, status 'stretch'
Hosting: AWS ECS on Fargate: $800-4,000 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) price band; x2 for 99.95% availability (redundant instances))

Database: PostgreSQL: $800-1,600 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) database tier (~500 GB in 12 months); upper end for ~500 GB of data: the band's top is priced for the largest data of the tier; x2 for 99.95% availability (standby/replicas))
Media delivery: $90-810 (~9,000 GB served a month (5 MB per active user a day) at $0.01-0.09/GB)
Phone login (SMS OTP): $180-450 (~90,000 SMS a month (one login every ~20 days per active user) at $0.002-0.005 each)
Static frontend: AWS S3 + CloudFront (static): $15-200 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) price band (the app's scale))
Model serving: CPU endpoint: $60-250 (one or two always-on small CPU instances behind a real-time endpoint (about $0.10-0.17 an hour each, https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/pricing/))

Sized for scale.users_12_months: 300,000 users, about 60,000 active on a day (20% daily-to-monthly ratio); scale.users_at_launch (10,000) is the starting point
rbi_localisation: RBI's 2018 directive on storage of payment system data requires payment data to be stored only in India, so every store must have an Indian region
iso27001: only hosts and managed services (backend-as-a-service, managed-only databases) that publish ISO/IEC 27001 certification are kept

compliance: DPDP Act 2023 (in force through the DPDP Rules 2025, notified November 2025 and phased in over 18 months) allows cross-border transfer except to notified countries, so it adds consent/breach-notice duties but not an India-region filter.
